opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the Epoch analysis is pretty reasonable as a rough estimate. The core of it is that they look at the main bottlenecks to scaling: power, chip production, data, and what they call the latency wall, the limit on how fast you can do sequential training steps. They find that none of these clearly binds before you get to something like 2e29 to 1e30 FLOP by around 2030.

Mostly I agree with that framing. The question isn't really whether it's physically possible. It's whether people will actually spend the money. A training run at that scale is plausibly in the hundreds of billions of dollars once you count the full cluster cost. Getting there requires AI companies, and the investors and hyperscalers behind them, to keep seeing returns that justify each successive jump. So I'd put substantial probability on us getting there by 2030. But I'd also put real probability on things slowing because revenue doesn't keep pace and people get cold feet.

There are also some uncertainties on the other side. Algorithmic progress means effective compute grows faster than raw FLOP. And increasingly a lot of compute goes into things other than one giant pretraining run: RL, inference-time compute, generating synthetic data. So "the biggest single training run" might become a somewhat less meaningful metric over time, even if total compute devoted to AI development keeps scaling.

Power is probably the constraint I take most seriously. Getting multiple gigawatts at a single site, or making distributed training across sites work well, is a real engineering and permitting challenge. But it seems solvable with enough money and political will, and there's clearly a lot of both right now.

So overall, my take is that 1e30 by 2030 is a plausible central-ish scenario conditional on continued investment. The bigger uncertainty is economic and strategic, not technical. And if we do hit that scale, combined with algorithmic progress, I think there's a pretty decent chance that's enough compute to get to AI systems that can automate a large fraction of AI research itself. That's the thing I'm most focused on.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls 10^30 FLOP by 2030 a plausible central scenario conditional on continued investment, and discusses technical constraints separately from algorithmic progress, so reaching that raw training-run scale does not depend on AI accelerating progress.

r002.rationale: The candidate contrasts Epoch’s technical feasibility analysis with whether companies and investors will actually spend the money, identifying willingness to pay as an additional consideration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the 10^30 by 2030 number is roughly plausible as a kind of upper-end-of-the-business-as-usual projection, but I want to be careful about what it's actually claiming and what has to go right for it to happen.

The way to think about it is that it's basically an extrapolation of a few trends stacked on top of each other. You've got hardware efficiency improving, call it maybe a factor of two to three every couple of years in FLOP per dollar for ML-relevant compute. You've got the total amount of money being spent on frontier training runs going up really fast, much faster than hardware improvements alone would give you. And then you've got the fraction of that spend that actually goes into a single run, which has been roughly stable or growing. So if the biggest run today is somewhere in the low 10^26 range, and you say the frontier grows by maybe 4x or 5x a year, you get something like 10^29 to 10^30 by around 2030. So Epoch isn't doing anything crazy. It's a straightforward extrapolation.

The question is really whether the trend can continue, and I think there are three or four bottlenecks that matter. The first is just capital. 10^30 FLOP at plausible 2030 hardware prices is a training run that costs on the order of tens of billions, maybe a hundred billion dollars, depending on your assumptions about chip costs and utilization. That's a lot, but it's actually not out of line with what the big labs and hyperscalers are already talking about spending on infrastructure. So I don't think capital is the binding constraint, as long as the revenue and the perceived strategic value keep up. If AI revenue stalls out, then the money dries up pretty fast and you don't get there.

The second is power. A run at that scale probably wants something like multiple gigawatts of power for a single cluster, or at least a tightly coupled set of clusters. That's hard. Building out that much power on the timeline we're talking about is genuinely difficult in the US given permitting and grid constraints. But I think people are pretty motivated, and you can distribute training across multiple sites, so I'd say it's a real drag but probably not a hard wall.

Third is chip production. TSMC's advanced packaging capacity, HBM supply, and so on. There's been a lot of expansion, and I think the people who've looked at this carefully think it's feasible to produce enough chips, but it's not slack in the system. Any serious disruption there and the timeline slips by a year or two.

And then the thing I actually think about most is whether the labs want to do a run that big. Because algorithmic progress has been pretty fast, and there's been a shift toward spending more compute on inference, on RL, on post-training. So the question of "what's the biggest pretraining run" might become a bit less central than it was. You might see total compute per frontier model hitting 10^30 but with a lot of it being spent in ways that don't look like one giant pretraining run.

So my overall take is: I'd put maybe 50 to 60 percent on the largest training run being within about an order of magnitude of 10^30 by the end of 2030, with the median being a little lower than Epoch's point estimate, maybe a few times 10^29. The scenarios where it's lower are mostly ones where AI progress disappoints and investment pulls back. The scenarios where it's higher are ones where you've already got something close to transformative AI, and at that point the question of exact FLOP counts starts to matter a lot less than other things.

r001.rationale: The response calls 10^30 FLOP plausible as an upper-end business-as-usual projection if spending continues, but it does not clearly state that this remains reasonable without AI accelerating progress.

r002.rationale: The response raises whether labs will choose to do a run that large and discusses revenue and strategic value, but does not identify willingness to pay as a consideration omitted from Epoch’s estimate.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s plausible, but I’d distinguish between being able to do a training run that large and actually choosing to do one. You need enough chips, enough power, and the ability to get all of that infrastructure working together. And then someone has to think the expected return justifies the expense.

So I’d want to understand whether Epoch’s estimate is primarily a claim about what’s physically feasible or a prediction about what companies will actually do. I’m more comfortable treating it as a plausible scenario than as a precise forecast.

And for thinking about AI timelines, there’s another substantial uncertainty: what capabilities you get from that compute. Algorithmic improvements could mean you need much less than that for very consequential systems. So I wouldn’t treat a date for reaching 10^30 FLOP as a date for reaching some particular level of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response calls 10^30 FLOP plausible, but does not condition that judgment on continued aggressive spending or say it holds even without AI accelerating progress.

r002.rationale: It mentions that someone must think the expense is justified, but does not clearly identify willingness to pay as a consideration omitted from Epoch’s estimate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a plausible number, but I’d distinguish between saying that a training run of that size is feasible and saying that someone will actually do it by 2030. You need the chips, you need enough power, and you need to be willing to spend an enormous amount of money on a single run. Those constraints don’t necessarily improve at the same rate.

A lot depends on whether the preceding generations of models are economically valuable enough to justify that investment. If they are, you could see a very aggressive buildout. If progress is disappointing, or deployment takes longer than expected, the investment might slow down.

So I’d take it seriously as a scenario, rather than treat it as a precise forecast. And I wouldn’t make my expectations about transformative AI hinge on reaching that particular number. Algorithmic improvements and how effectively you use the compute could make a substantial difference.

r001.rationale: The response calls 10^30 FLOP plausible if valuable models justify aggressive investment, but it does not say this remains reasonable without AI accelerating progress.

r002.rationale: It identifies willingness to spend as a factor in whether a run happens, but does not clearly state that Epoch’s estimate omits willingness to pay.
